description: Food-contact safety guidance archived from Digitalfire ahead of the site's shutdown, primarily 'Are Your Glazes Food Safe or are They Leachable?' (digitalfire.com/article/12), plus oxide-specific hazard pages. This is guidance for spotting known risk patterns, not a certification - the article is explicit that only real leach testing (a lab, or the vinegar/dishwasher tests below) confirms whether a specific glaze is actually safe.
core_principle: A glaze is leachable when its glass network is not fully stable - primarily from being underfired, or from having inadequate SiO2/Al2O3 relative to its flux content ('flux saturation'). Concerning oxides (lead, barium, lithium, manganese, copper, chrome, cadmium) are dangerous specifically because an unstable glass releases them; a well-melted, properly formulated glaze holds them far more securely.

PbO.name: Lead
PbO.note: Any presence is a food-safety concern. FDA 1992 CPG set 4% acetic-acid leach limits (cups/mugs at 0.5 micrograms/mL, previously 5.0). Even fritted/leadless-labeled glazes can leach if the glass itself is unstable. Quantified: adding just 1% copper oxide to a 50%-lead-bisilicate glaze raised measured lead release from 0.1ppm to 12.8ppm (a 128x increase) in published leach testing; a leadless (0% lead bisilicate) glaze with the same copper addition stayed at 0.1ppm. The effect scales with lead content - a 90%-lead-bisilicate base only rose to 0.8ppm with 1% copper. Ceramic stains (fritted oxide/carbonate blends) showed far less impact on lead release than raw copper oxide at the same addition rate.

BaO.name: Barium
BaO.note: Like lead, leaches from improperly formulated or fired surfaces. Art-glaze levels of ~20-50% BaCO3 (matte/stony-matte effects) are almost certainly leachable. Strontium (SrO) is a non-hazardous substitute for its flux/color effects; calcia (CaO) can substitute for its matting effect.

Li2O.name: Lithium
Li2O.note: High lithium carbonate (>5% of the batch) is a specific red flag named in the source article, distinct from lithium-bearing feldspars like spodumene at typical percentages.

CuO.name: Copper
CuO.note: Copper is well known to destabilize other metals in the fired glass and specifically increases lead solubility. A 10:10 ratio with manganese is called out as a specific heavy-metal leaching risk. 2% copper carbonate is cited as passing leaching tests in a well-formulated glaze - the concern is high concentrations and interaction with other colorants, not copper's mere presence. People with Wilson's disease should avoid it entirely.

MnO2.name: Manganese
MnO2.note: Public drinking water standards cited at 0.01-0.05 mg/liter as a benchmark. Combines with copper at high concentration as a specific leaching risk (see CuO). Separately a serious inhalation hazard during firing - see handling_hazards.

Cr2O3.name: Chrome
Cr2O3.note: Named alongside lead/barium/lithium/manganese/copper/cadmium as a substance requiring caution on food-contact surfaces. Not tracked in this app's UMF model.

CdO.name: Cadmium
CdO.note: Named as a concerning oxide. Not tracked anywhere in this app's chemistry model - cadmium-selenium stains produce some bright reds/oranges/yellows and their exact formulation is manufacturer-specific. Check the SDS for saturated warm-color stains used on functional ware.

chemistry_risk_factors.underfired: If a glaze is not properly melted it will be leachable, regardless of its recipe. Test firing +/- 2 cones to confirm adequate melt.
chemistry_risk_factors.low_glass_formers: Inadequate SiO2 and Al2O3 relative to flux content is the single biggest chemistry driver of leaching - the same low-silica/low-alumina condition this app's chemistry analysis already flags as an 'issue' for other reasons (matte/dry surface, running) also means less capacity to hold colorants securely.
chemistry_risk_factors.flux_saturation: Excess feldspar (the article's example: 50%+) leaves too little silica/alumina to secure colorants even with normal-looking flux oxides.
chemistry_risk_factors.excess_talc: More than ~5% talc is named as a specific formulation red flag.
chemistry_risk_factors.high_boron_frit_high_fire: More than ~10% boron frit is unusual and flagged as suspicious specifically in high-fire (roughly cone 6+) glazes, where that much low-temperature flux is atypical.
chemistry_risk_factors.crazing: Crazing (fine surface cracks) shares its root cause with leaching - low silica/alumina relative to flux, causing high thermal expansion. A crazed surface is also porous enough to harbor bacteria independent of any metal leaching.

testing_methods.dishwasher_test: Compare an identical piece left in a cupboard against one run through ~2 months of dishwasher cycles. Changes in color, gloss or texture indicate vulnerability to base attack.
testing_methods.vinegar_test: Fill a glazed container halfway with vinegar (lemon juice is stronger) and leave several days; compare the surface above and below the liquid line. Adding 5% cobalt to an otherwise white/transparent glaze amplifies the visible effect - an unstable version may turn white after overnight leaching.
testing_methods.lab_testing: Acidic solution held in contact with the glaze, then analyzed for trace metals. Individual metal tests typically run $30-60 each.

safe_formulation_guidance: A 'liner glaze' (clear/white interior food-contact surface, no added color) made from kaolin, ball clay, bentonite, silica, feldspar and calcium-based fluxes is the safest general approach.
Frits are safe as long as they contain no lead or barium - check the frit's own analysis.

Prefer ceramic stains over raw metal oxide colorants for functional ware; stains are sintered colorant/stabilizer blends and need far less raw material to achieve the same color than something like 15% raw manganese/cobalt/nickel/iron blends.

MnO2.note: Manganese fume during firing is a more serious hazard than the dust - a standard dust mask does not filter it, and open-air/outdoor firing is not sufficient protection on its own. Needs a respirator rated for metal fumes specifically. Source is a first-person account of chronic manganese toxicity from raku firing, not a regulatory standard - treated here as a strong cautionary note, not a numeric limit.

CuO.note: OSHA rates copper dust as a relatively low hazard (TLV 1.0 mg/m3 - higher/safer than quartz's 0.05-0.1, lower/more hazardous than barium carbonate's 0.5) but it is an airborne irritant, and volatilized copper during firing can cause temporary metal fume fever.
